scenes.narration: Fifty million dollars.
That was the price tag on Netflix.
And Blockbuster said no.
Today, Netflix is worth hundreds of billions.
Blockbuster? Down to one store. In Oregon.
Dumbest no in business history? Not quite.
By the end, you'll see why saying no made sense.
And the boardroom fight, seven years later, that most retellings skip.
Dallas, Texas.
Blockbuster headquarters. The year is two thousand.
Blockbuster was born right here in Dallas, in nineteen eighty-five.
Now it rules home video.
Thousands of stores.
Close to five billion dollars a year in revenue.
And still growing, up about eleven percent.
The boss is John Antioco.
A retail lifer. Around twenty years at Seven-Eleven. Then Circle K. Then Taco Bell.
In nineteen ninety-seven, he took the top job at Blockbuster.
Antioco knows how to make stores pay.
In the building: three visitors from California.
Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph, who founded Netflix in nineteen ninety-seven.
And their finance chief, Barry McCarthy.
Their idea? A video rental shop with no shop.
DVDs by mail. You pick films on a website. The discs land in your mailbox.
Since September nineteen ninety-nine, one flat monthly fee.
And DVD is spreading fast.
By the end of the next year, about twenty-five million American homes will own a player. Nearly double.

scenes.narration: Now look at Netflix's own numbers for two thousand. About three hundred thousand subscribers.
Revenue: thirty-five point nine million dollars.
And the loss: fifty-seven point four million.
Netflix spends far more than it earns.
Remember that number. Because then the Netflix team names its price.
Fifty million dollars.
Every version of this story agrees on that number.
Almost everything else is disputed.
Who was in the room. What was said. Even the month. Hold on to that.
So you're in Antioco's chair.
First, the case for saying no.
Reason one: the math. Netflix is on its way to losing more this year than its own price tag.
And buying a company means buying its losses. Next year too. And the year after.
Nobody can promise when it will turn a profit.

props.text: WHEN WOULD IT TURN A PROFIT?

scenes.narration: Reason two: the mood. In two thousand, the dot-com bubble peaked and began to burst.
Internet companies that lost money were suddenly suspect.
Netflix was exactly that kind of company.
Reason three: scale. About three hundred thousand subscribers against thousands of stores.
Why bet on a tiny website when your own shops are still growing?
Reason four: who really decides? Blockbuster's parent company is the media giant Viacom.
Could Antioco buy Netflix on his own? We simply don't know.
Sounds like an easy no. But here's where it gets interesting.
Fifty million was about one percent of Blockbuster's yearly revenue. Small change for a giant.
The risk wasn't the price. It was the idea.
A rental business with no stores. No shelves. No counters. No store rent.
And if renting by mail caught on? Customers might stop walking into Blockbuster at all.
For one percent of a year's revenue, it could own the thing. The thing that might replace it.

lines: OWN THE THING THAT MIGHT REPLACE IT

scenes.narration: Cheap insurance? Or an expensive distraction?
So here it is.
A start-up losing more than its own price tag. Your own business, still growing.
Fifty million dollars on the table.
Would you sign? Comment SIGN or PASS before I tell you.
[pause 1] Blockbuster passed. No deal.
But how that no happened depends on who you ask. And this is where it gets strange.
Marc Randolph tells the famous version. In his twenty nineteen book, That Will Never Work, he recalls Antioco struggling not to laugh.
In twenty twenty-three, he wrote on Twitter that Blockbuster "laughed us out of the room."

visual.text: laughed us out of the room
visual.speaker: Marc Randolph, on Twitter, 2023 (his recollection)

scenes.narration: That's how Randolph remembers it.
John Antioco remembers it very differently.
In twenty twenty-one, he wrote on LinkedIn:
"I can say with complete confidence that there were never any serious acquisition talks in 2000."

visual.text: I can say with complete confidence that there were never any serious acquisition talks in 2000.
visual.speaker: John Antioco, on LinkedIn, 2021

scenes.narration: He says he wasn't even in the meeting. He only stopped by to greet the guests.
And Reed Hastings? He has reportedly said he doesn't think it was serious. More curiosity than anything else.
Three men. Three memories. Told nearly twenty years later, or more.
Only three things are certain. A meeting in Dallas. A number: fifty million. And no deal.
But that's not the crazy part. Watch what happens next.
Netflix keeps going. In May two thousand and two, it goes public.
Its shares hit the stock market at fifteen dollars each.
At that price, the whole company is valued at about three hundred and ten million dollars.
Six times its Dallas price tag.
The offering alone raises eighty-two and a half million. More than Blockbuster was asked to pay.

visual.label: Raised in the IPO, $15 a share

scenes.narration: By then, it has more than six hundred thousand subscribers. About double what it had in two thousand.
More than eleven and a half thousand titles. Nineteen dollars ninety-five a month.
And Blockbuster? Here's the part almost everyone skips. Blockbuster fights back.
In two thousand and four, it hits its peak. Nine thousand and ninety-four stores.
And eighty-four thousand three hundred employees.
That same year, it splits from Viacom. And launches its own online service: Blockbuster Online.
January two thousand and five. It drops most late fees, the fines for bringing a movie back late.
Meanwhile, a new player has arrived.
Since late two thousand and four, the activist investor Carl Icahn has been buying in.
That's an investor who buys in to shake things up. He builds a stake of nearly ten percent.

lines: BUYS IN TO SHAKE THINGS UP

scenes.narration: In May two thousand and five, he wins a seat on the board.
And the numbers turn ugly. For two thousand and five: a net loss of five hundred and eighty-eight million dollars.
More than half is a write-down. An admission that some assets were worth less than the books said.
Then, in autumn two thousand and six, Blockbuster plays its best card. Total Access.
Rent online. Return the disc to a Blockbuster store. Swap it for a free rental.
Netflix has no stores. It can't match that.
And it works.
By the end of two thousand and six: about two point two million online subscribers.
Seven hundred thousand added in three months alone. The target: three million by the end of March.

visual.label: Added in Q4 2006 (target: 3M by end of March)

scenes.narration: And Blockbuster is back in profit. Fifty-four point seven million dollars.
Antioco says Netflix came back to the table.
Serious talks, he says, in early two thousand and seven. That's his account.
So Blockbuster has a shot? Not so fast. Here's the boardroom fight I promised you.
January two thousand and seven. The board offers Antioco a bonus of two point two eight million dollars.
He says he's owed seven point six five million.
In March, they settle. His lump-sum exit payment: just under five million.
His old contract would have paid thirteen and a half million.
That summer, Jim Keyes takes over as CEO. The man who launched Total Access is gone.
That same year, Netflix starts streaming. Films over the internet. No disc at all.
Now the fall.
Twenty-third of September, two thousand and ten. Blockbuster files for Chapter Eleven, American bankruptcy protection.
In two thousand and eleven, Dish Network buys it out of bankruptcy. About seventeen hundred stores.
In early two thousand and fourteen, the last company-owned stores close.
Today, one Blockbuster is still open.
A single franchised store. In Bend, Oregon.
And Netflix? In twenty twenty-five, revenue of forty-five point two billion dollars.
About nine hundred times that fifty million price tag.
Profit: eleven billion dollars. And a company worth hundreds of billions.
So did one no in Dallas kill Blockbuster? Probably not on its own.
Blockbuster did fight for the online future. For a while, it was gaining ground.
Would owning Netflix have saved it? Nobody can know.
Fifty million dollars, on the table in Dallas. [pause 0.4] Blockbuster passed.
When a small company could replace your core business, don't just ask what it's worth today.

metadata.description:
In 2000, a money-losing start-up that mailed DVDs to people's homes named its price: $50 million. The company across the table had thousands of stores and close to $5 billion in yearly revenue. Blockbuster did not buy Netflix.

Today Netflix is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and Blockbuster is down to one franchised store in Bend, Oregon. But the story is more complicated than the legend. Three people remember that meeting in Dallas in three different ways. Sit in John Antioco's chair and decide for yourself.

Would you have signed? Tell us in the comments.
